strengths: Targets an important and under-explored issue in MLLMs: cross-modal information flow in decoder-only architectures, showing how causal attention limits image tokens from accessing later text queries.

Proposes a simple, parameter-free attention-mask modification (Modality-Mutual Attention) that can be integrated into existing MLLM training pipelines without extra parameters, and formulates a generalized mask for multiple modalities/interleaved data.
Provides extensive evaluation on 12 multimodal benchmarks and reports consistent gains over CCA and dual-order training variants on 11/12 benchmarks under a controlled short-schedule comparison.

Implementation details are relatively thorough: hyperparameters, data mixtures, prompt templates, and qualitative examples are provided, and the broader impacts/limitations section acknowledges the PT-stage leakage issue.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is not fully specified: Eq. (5) lets image tokens attend to all text tokens up to |V|+|T_Q|, but it is unclear whether T_Q includes answer/response tokens during SFT. If image tokens attend to answer tokens, this creates severe information leakage and invalidates the reported gains; if they attend only to question tokens, the method is essentially question-conditioned visual encoding and the paper should clearly state/ablate this distinction.

Table 1 compares under a short training schedule with no seeds, error bars, or statistical tests, and DOT performs suspiciously poorly on MMB/SEED (e.g., 43.8 vs. 64.9 for the standard baseline). This suggests the dual-order baselines may be undertrained or misconfigured, so the comparisons do not reliably isolate the benefit of MMA.

State-of-the-art claims in Table 2 are not supported by apples-to-apples comparisons: AKI-4B is evaluated against models with vastly different pretraining data, resolutions, and vision-token budgets, and many baseline numbers are copied from leaderboards rather than re-evaluated. AKI-4B is best on only a minority of 3B/4B metrics, and the claim of outperforming 7B-scale MLLMs rests on only two 7B baselines.

The average improvement claim (+7.2%) is not consistently defined and may be inflated by averaging heterogeneous MME sub-scores; on RealWorldQA MMA is slightly worse than CCA, and gains on SEED/MMB are modest.

Originality is limited: attention-mask modifications and cross-modal visibility changes are well known in prefix-LM/early-fusion multimodal transformers. The specific image-to-text direction is intuitive rather than conceptually new, and the paper offers no theoretical analysis of why this should be sufficient for vision-language misalignment.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code URL ('available at ,'), lack of training seeds/variance, and insufficient description of how the attention mask interacts with teacher forcing and generated response tokens during training.

The paper's strongest empirical support for MMA is against CCA, a hallucination-mitigation baseline, not against the strongest standard MLLM baselines under matched compute/data. Thus the practical significance of the design over existing alternatives remains unclear.

strengths: The core intervention is genuinely simple and cheap: modifying the LLM attention mask so image tokens can attend to the question tokens requires no extra parameters and no extra training time, and can be dropped into existing MLLM pipelines. This is an appealing, low-cost architectural lever.

The paper attacks a real and important problem (vision-language misalignment / object hallucination) from an architectural angle rather than only via data scaling or connector design, which is a reasonable and useful framing.

The evaluation is broad (12 benchmarks spanning general, knowledge, and vision-centric tasks), and asking all compared methods (baseline, CCA, DOT, variants) to be retrained under identical data/configurations is good practice for apples-to-apples comparison, even if the numbers are not always faithful (see weaknesses).

The paper is well-motivated and readable, includes detailed appendices (hyperparameters, prompt templates, dataset statistics, per-category scores), and commits to releasing code and the AKI-4B model, which supports reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: Novelty and framing are overstated. Letting image tokens attend to text tokens is a small mask change closely related to prefix-LM/bidirectional-prompt attention and to CCA (which the paper itself cites as SOTA). Presenting it as a 'fundamental yet unexplored perspective' is not supported by any serious discussion of prior attention-mask/bidirectional-attention work.

There are internal numerical inconsistencies that undermine trust in the results. For MMA, MME^P is reported as 1363.7 in Table 1 but the perception sum in Table 7 is 1344.9, and MMB is 71.8 in Table 1 vs 70.3 in Table 8. (The analogous AKI-4B numbers do match, so the MMA row is the problem.) These are not explained.

The DOT baseline appears broken rather than merely worse: it collapses on general benchmarks (e.g., MMB 43.8 vs 64.9 for the standard pipeline, SEED 54.7 vs 64.1) while slightly helping some vision-centric tasks. The paper's central narrative ('intuitive approach' vs. MMA) rests on a comparison against a strawman whose catastrophic regression is attributed hand-wavily to 'confusing' image positions.

The headline '+7.2% on average' is computed relative to the reimplemented CCA baseline, not the standard (I&T)+(I&T) pipeline, and it silently excludes RealWorldQA (where CCA actually beats MMA, 52.7 vs 52.3) via the blank in the improvements row. This is a misleading way to present the main quantitative claim.

The specific mask design is never ablated and no alternative attention modifications are compared. It is not shown that image->text attention (rather than, e.g., full bidirectional attention among prompt tokens, or simply different training) is responsible for the gains; no analysis (attention statistics, ablation of which tokens attend to which) supports the mechanism.

Generality and reproducibility are limited: a single backbone (Phi-3.5-mini), single connector (Perceiver Resampler), and single vision encoder (SigLIP). The controlled comparison (Section 4.2) uses a very short schedule (50k PT / 5k SFT), so it is unclear how much of the effect survives at scale or with other architectures.

The method cannot be used during pretraining (acknowledged due to leakage), so the gains depend on a short SFT adaptation stage; this limits the reach of the claimed 'generic and scalable' design and raises the question of whether improvements reflect a fundamental fix or a narrow fine-tuning artifact.

The AKI-4B comparisons vs. state-of-the-art are weakened by a different (much smaller) data/resolution/vision-token budget, and the conclusion that it 'outperforms 7B-scale MLLMs' is drawn from a small, self-selected set of baselines; the aggregate picture of significance is not fully convincing.

strengths: The proposed modality-mutual attention (MMA) is a simple, parameter-free architectural modification that can be integrated into existing MLLM training pipelines by changing only the attention mask.

The controlled apples-to-apples comparison in Table 1 is the paper's strongest evidence: under the same training data and schedules, MMA consistently improves over the causal baseline, DOT variants, and CCA across most of the 12 benchmarks.

The paper provides useful ablations of dual-order training and detailed appendix material, including hyperparameters, prompt templates, per-benchmark scores, and qualitative examples, which supports reproducibility.
The limitation section honestly discusses that MMA currently benefits the SFT stage and would cause leakage if applied to the PT stage, which is an appropriate treatment of scope.
The idea is generalizable in formulation to other modalities and interleaved settings, even though this is not empirically tested.
weaknesses: The abstract promises a public code link, but the URL is missing/blank in the manuscript, which weakens verifiability despite the detailed appendix.

The SOTA comparison in Table 2 is overclaimed: AKI-4B does not outperform several 2B/4B open-source models (e.g., Qwen2-VL-2B, BLIP-3-4B) on many benchmarks, and the 7B comparison uses only two older baselines, making the 'outperforms 7B-scale MLLMs' claim narrow.
The evaluation relies on single training runs without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; several reported gains over CCA are small (1-4%) and could be within noise.
Only one LLM backbone/model scale (Phi-3.5-mini 4B) is evaluated, so the scaling behavior and generality of MMA remain unclear.

The paper does not ablate against other plausible input-attention designs, such as full bidirectional attention over the image+text prompt, so it is unclear whether the specific image-to-text unlock is optimal.

The claim of no training-time increase may depend on implementation: custom non-causal masks can reduce the efficiency of optimized causal attention kernels, and this overhead is not discussed or measured.

The formal mask assumes image tokens are positions 1..|V|, but the actual prompt templates include system/user text tokens before the image; how MMA is aligned with special tokens and prompt formatting is not fully specified.
The broader multi-modality and interleaved-data claims are only formulated, not evaluated, so their practical benefit remains speculative.
